query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles, slight nanoscale compositional fluctuations produce local variations in metal–metal cohesive energy that cause regions enriched in the lower cohesive energy element (Cu) to undergo premelting at temperatures below the global melting point. This localized premelting triggers early defect formation and melting heterogeneity that governs the overall thermal response of the nanoparticles.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid high-entropy alloy nanoparticles with an overall homogeneous distribution of Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu, but with inevitable nanoscale compositional fluctuations.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled heating protocol across the premelting and melting temperature regimes, followed by controlled cooling to consolidate the solid solution.
generation.conditions: Experiments performed under an inert atmosphere with a constant heating rate and precise temperature control, ensuring that observed effects are due to intrinsic alloy behavior rather than environmental oxidation or contamination.
generation.structural_mediator: Local elemental segregation at the nanoscale that results in spatial variations of metal–metal cohesive energies; specifically, Cu-enriched regions serve as nucleation sites for premature softening/melting.
generation.mechanism: The differential cohesive energies among the constituent metals mean that, where minor Cu enrichment exists, the local bonding is weaker. Under thermal stress, these regions begin melting before the rest of the nanoparticle, creating defects and initiating a cascade that drives the overall phase transition. This heterogeneous premelting contrasts with the more uniform melting observed in single-metal nanoparticles.
generation.predicted_outcome: In situ thermal analysis (e.g., TEM with compositional mapping) will show that melting initiates in localized regions that correlate with higher Cu concentration. Compared to a homogeneous nanoparticle baseline (or single-element nanoparticles), the HEA nanoparticles will display a staggered melting profile, with detectable premelting occurring at a lower temperature in these weakly bonded regions.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles of a single metal or binary alloy that display a uniform melting transition without pronounced localized premelting phase initiation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be significant in nanoparticles at the nanoscale (<10 nm) where compositional fluctuations are not fully averaged out and for high-entropy alloys specifically composed of Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu. It may not apply at larger scales or in alloy systems with less disparity in individual metal cohesive energies.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative relationship between the local Cu concentration and the magnitude of the melting point depression is not fully established, and the threshold level of compositional fluctuation required to trigger observable premelting remains to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ heating transmission electron microscopy (TEM) experiments on Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu HEA nanoparticles while simultaneously mapping local composition (e.g., via energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy) to track the onset and spatial distribution of premelting. Compare these observations to control experiments on homogeneous single-metal or binary alloy nanoparticles.
measurements: Temperature-resolved TEM imaging of nanoparticle morphology
Spatially resolved compositional mapping (EDX/EELS) to identify areas with elevated Cu concentration
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to detect staggered melting transitions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If premelting does not preferentially initiate in regions of relatively higher Cu concentration—that is, if melting occurs uniformly across the nanoparticles without correlation to local compositional fluctuations—then the hypothesis that nanoscale cohesive energy variations control the premelting behavior is falsified.

The more the better: on the formation of single-phase high entropy alloy nanoparticles as catalysts for the oxygen reduction reaction†

Abstract: AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) are an important new material class with significant application potential in catalysis and electrocatalysis. The entropy-driven formation of HEA materials requires high temperatures and controlled cooling rates. However, catalysts in general also require highly dispersed materials, i.e., nanoparticles. Only then a favorable utilization of the expensive raw materials can be achieved. Several recently reported HEA nanoparticle synthesis strategies, therefore, avoid the high-temperature regime to prevent particle growth. In our work, we investigate a system of five noble metal single-source precursors with superior catalytic activity for the oxygen reduction reaction. Combining in situ X-ray powder diffraction with multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy, we address the fundamental question of how single-phase HEA nanoparticles can form at low temperatures. Periodicity in the Electrochemical Dissolution of Transition Metals

Abstract: AbstractExtensive research efforts are currently dedicated to the search for new electrocatalyst materials in which expensive and rare noble metals are replaced with cheaper and more abundant transition metals. Recently, numerous alloys, oxides, and composites with such metals have been identified as highly active electrocatalysts through the use of high‐throughput screening methods with the help of activity descriptors. Up to this point, stability has lacked such descriptors. Hence, we elucidate the role of intrinsic metal/oxide properties on the corrosion behavior of representative 3d, 4d, and 5d transition metals. Electrochemical dissolution of nine transition metals is quantified using online inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP‐MS). Based on the obtained dissolution data in alkaline and acidic media, we establish clear periodic correlations between the amount of dissolved metal, the cohesive energy of the metal atoms (E coh), and the energy of oxygen adsorption on the metal (ΔH O,ads). Such correlations can support the knowledge‐driven search for more stable electrocatalysts.Keywords: c
